title: How to design an MVP that feels finished
excerpt: MVP design feels finished when one workflow is polished, including the empty screen, the error, and the success. A wide product with rough edges does not.
alt: Two white smartwatch mockups on a plain light background, one showing the face and one the back. A finished object is complete on the sides people actually see.
caption: Finish the path people will actually touch. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What makes an MVP feel finished instead of merely small?
faqs.answer: A finished MVP has one workflow a new person can complete, plus the empty screen, the success, and the failure. The edges of that path are deliberate. A small product that still requires the founder to say which buttons to ignore is a rough draft with fewer buttons.

faqs.question: Which states should we design before launch?
faqs.answer: Design the blank account, the moment the main action succeeds, and the failures you can actually cause, such as a rejected field or a lost connection. A populated demo screen is the easy picture. The first real customer will not have that data.

faqs.question: How do we cut scope without looking like we quit?
faqs.answer: Keep a written later list so postponed ideas are not lost. The version you ship should fit on one page and include the empty, success, and error states. If a feature cannot receive those states in the time you have, it belongs on the later list.

markdown:
MVP design feels finished when one narrow path is polished. That path includes the empty screen, the error, the success, and the single workflow a person came to complete. The unfinished shape is the reverse: many workflows, each of them rough. Small is not the same as done. Done is a short road someone can walk without falling through a missing step.

Founders are often told to ship something and then apologize for it in the demo. The apology is a clue. If you have to explain which buttons to ignore, the path is wider than the care you had time to give it. Cut the width until the remaining path can be cared for. A customer can forgive a missing feature. They have a harder time forgiving a feature that looks ready and then breaks.

## Name the one workflow

Write the workflow as a sequence of decisions, not as a wishlist of screens. A person arrives with a purpose, does the thing, and leaves with a result they can trust. For an early product that might be creating a lead and knowing it was saved, or seeing today's exceptions and marking one as handled.

Everything off that sequence waits. Write the waiting down, so it does not return as a link in the corner. A corner link is how a small build becomes a tour of unfinished rooms. Each room asks for a sentence, an empty state, and an error you do not have time to write.

The workflow should be finishable by someone other than you, using the labels on the screen. If it requires a spoken preface, it is still a prototype. Prototypes are useful in a meeting. They are a poor thing to hand a first customer under the name of a product. The difference is whether the screen can carry the preface by itself.

## Polish the states people actually meet

The happy path is the easiest picture and the least honest test. Specify four situations before you call the workflow done.

**Empty.** The person has arrived and there is nothing here yet. The screen should say what this place is and offer the one action that fills it. A blank table with no sentence assumes yesterday's data. New accounts do not have yesterday.

**In progress.** The person is halfway through. They can tell what is saved, what is still required, and how to go back without losing the work. A spinner with no words is not a state. It is a pause that might be a failure.

**Success.** The action worked. Say what happened and what the person can do next, in concrete nouns. "Saved" is weaker than "Saved to today's list." The next step should be a real place in the product, not a generic cheer.

**Error.** The action failed, or the person missed a rule you set. Say what went wrong and what to do, next to the thing that broke. The W3C organizes WCAG under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. Conformance means meeting testable success criteria, not a general impression that the screen feels modern. [The WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is the reference when you want that standard named. An understandable error is part of a finished path. A red border with no words is a rough edge on the only road you claimed to pave.

## What a rough product looks like in a demo

You can hear unfinished work. The presenter says "ignore that" more than once. Each ignore is a control that was included before it was ready. Remove it until the demo can be quiet. Silence is a good test. If the path needs a narrator, the path is not finished.

A finished narrow product can still be small. One list, one detail, one action. Buttons do what their labels say. The empty list teaches the action. The error tells the truth. The success confirms the result in the same words as the button. That is a product a stranger can try on the first afternoon, which is the only afternoon some of them will give you.

Settings pages are a common place the roughness hides. Twelve toggles, none of them tried on a phone, signal a second product. Leave settings out until a real workflow demands one switch, and design that switch with the same four situations. A toggle that fails silently is not a small feature. It is a broken promise in a corner.

## How to cut without losing the idea

Make a column for this version and a column for later. The later column is allowed to be long. The this-version column should fit on a page and should include the empty, the success, and the error. If a feature cannot be given those states in the time you have, it belongs in later. Postponing it is a decision. Forgetting it in a comment thread is how it returns half-built.

Build in the order a person meets the product. Start with empty, because that is launch day for every new account. Then the workflow. Then success. Then the failures you can actually produce: a rejected field, a lost connection, a missing permission. Teams that start from a populated demo and never design the blank screen are surprised by the first real signup. The surprise is avoidable. It is a frame in the file.

Hanabi builds interfaces in production code, with React and TypeScript, once the path is clear enough that more picture-making would hide the states. A state you have not implemented is a state you have only imagined. Imagined errors tend to say "something went wrong," which is not a thing a person can act on. The sentence is the design. The component is how you find out the sentence is too long, or missing.

## A check before a customer sees it

Walk the path as a new account. Use a phone if the product will be used on a phone. Read every word you meet. Take the one action. Force one error. Reach the success and read it without talking. Then ask someone who has the job to do the same, without your narration.

Where they stop, the path is not finished, even if the populated screenshot looks complete. Fix that spot before you add the next workflow. Adding width to avoid a hard sentence is how the product stays rough everywhere.

The practical way to keep the path short enough to finish is to cut screens that do not add a decision. Read [fewer screens, a clearer product](/blog/fewer-screens-clearer-product) for that cut. A hallway of steps will spread your care too thin to feel finished.
